LO 1

Describe contributions of host, infectious agent, and environment to infectious disease

The Epidemiological Triad — all three must interact for disease to occur.

  • ✓
    Host → age, immune status, genetics, nutrition, prior exposure, occupation, living conditions
  • ✓
    Agent → virulence, infectivity, dose, resistance to host defenses, survival in environment
  • ✓
    Environment → climate, sanitation, population density, healthcare infrastructure
  • ✓
    Infectious dose: some agents need 1–10 organisms (Bordetella pertussis); others need 108
LO 1

The Epidemiological Triad

Host, Infectious Agent & Environment

The occurrence of infectious disease depends on the dynamic interaction of three factors forming the Epidemiological Triad. All three must align for disease to develop.

Slide — ID Occurrence Based on Interaction of Host, Agent & Environment

🧑‍⚕️

Host Factors

  • Age (extremes: <5 and >60 are highest risk)
  • Individual hygiene and living conditions
  • Travel history and occupation
  • Immune and nutritional status
  • Underlying diseases (DM, HIV, malignancy)
  • Prior exposure / vaccination history
  • Genetic factors
🦠

Infectious Agent Factors

  • Virulence — capacity to cause disease
  • Infectivity — ability to establish infection
  • Infectious dose — number of organisms required
  • Resistance to immune responses (humoral & cellular)
  • Resistance to antibiotics
  • Survival in host and in the environment
🌍 Environmental Factors
Climate (temperature, humidity, pH), dust (major vehicle for transmission), level of sanitation, population density, physical structures, and overall healthcare of the population.
💡 Infectious Dose Concept
Some pathogens require only 1–10 organisms (Bordetella pertussis). Others require 108. Lower dose = more easily contagious.

Q: A patient asks why her immunocompromised neighbor got sick after minimal exposure while she remained healthy. What triad concept explains this?

Answer

The Epidemiological Triad: the neighbor's compromised host immune status (host factor) combined with even a low dose of the infectious agent in the same environment allowed disease to develop, while the patient's intact immune system prevented infection despite the same environmental exposure.

LO 2

Define commensalism, mutualism, and parasitism

Three types of host-microorganism relationships. Know who benefits and who is harmed.

  • ✓
    Commensalism → no benefit or harm to either party; can become pathogenic if barriers broken (e.g., Staph epidermidis on skin → systemic if IV line introduced)
  • ✓
    Mutualism → both benefit; vaginal Lactobacilli produce acid → inhibits Candida and BV organisms
  • ✓
    Parasitism → organism grows at expense of host; host gains nothing; includes both indigenous transient flora (Strep pneumo) and non-indigenous pathogens (TB, typhoid)
LO 2

Host-Parasite Relationships

Commensalism, Mutualism & Parasitism

Slide — Host/Parasite Interactions

RelationshipHost Benefit?Microbe Benefit?Classic Example
CommensalismNeutral (no harm)Yes (sheltered)Staph epidermidis on normal skin — 95–97% of skin flora
Mutualism (Symbiosis)YesYesVaginal Lactobacilli: host provides glycogen → bacteria produce acid → host gets protection from Candida & BV
ParasitismNoYesStrep pneumo, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae as transient flora; TB, typhoid as non-indigenous
⚠️ Commensals Can Become Pathogens
Staph epidermidis is harmless on intact skin but causes serious systemic infection when introduced via IV lines or catheters in hospitalized (immunocompromised) patients.
🩺 Antibiotic-Induced Yeast Infections
Antibiotics kill off vaginal Lactobacilli, reducing acid → Candida albicans thrives → vaginal yeast infection. Classic: young woman with UTI treated with antibiotics develops vaginal candidiasis.

Q: 15–20% of people carry Streptococcus pneumoniae in their upper respiratory tract with no symptoms. What type of host-parasite interaction is this?

Answer

Parasitism — the organism is sheltered, provides nothing useful, and is assumed to eventually have the potential to cause disease. These are transient indigenous parasitic organisms.

LO 3

Describe the categories of infectious disease

Know definitions precisely — especially nosocomial vs. iatrogenic, and subclinical vs. latent.

  • ✓
    Communicable = transmitted from a source (animate/inanimate)
  • ✓
    Contagious = highly communicable; low infectious dose; direct/close contact
  • ✓
    Nosocomial = healthcare-acquired; ~100,000 deaths/year in US
  • ✓
    Iatrogenic = subset of nosocomial; caused by medical intervention (lines, catheters, surgery)
  • ✓
    Opportunistic = low virulence agent in immunocompromised host
  • ✓
    Subclinical = immune response occurs, no symptoms, but person IS shedding organism
  • ✓
    Latent = organism dormant/hidden, not detectable, not shedding (herpes, TB)
  • ✓
    Zoonosis = animal pathogen → human; >200 known; via vector bite or direct contact
  • ✓
    Emerging/Re-emerging = newly appeared or rapidly increasing (COVID, Mpox)
LO 3

Classification

Categories of Infectious Disease

Slide — Categories of Infectious Diseases

CategoryDefinitionKey Example
CommunicableTransmitted from an animate or inanimate external source to a patientMost respiratory and GI pathogens
ContagiousHighly communicable; typically low infectious dose; direct/close contact spreadMeasles, pertussis (1–10 organisms)
NosocomialAcquired in a healthcare facility; ~100,000 deaths/year in the USMRSA, CLABSI, CAUTI
IatrogenicSubset of nosocomial; caused by actual medical interventionPost-surgical wound infection, catheter-associated UTI
OpportunisticLow-virulence organism → causes infection only in immunocompromised hostPneumocystis jirovecii in AIDS
SubclinicalImmunologic response occurs but NO clinical symptoms; organism is being shed — person CAN transmit!Norovirus shedding for 4 weeks post-illness
Secondary InfectionOccurs during or after recovery from a preceding infectionBacterial pneumonia following influenza
Latent InfectionAgent dormant/hidden; no signs, no symptoms, not detectable. Can reactivate.Herpes (dorsal root ganglia), TB (walled off 30–40 years)
ZoonosisAnimal pathogens spread to humans; >200 established diseasesRabies, Lyme, Mpox, COVID, plague, anthrax
Emerging/Re-emergingNewly recognized or rapidly increasing incidence / geographic spreadCOVID-19, Mpox, H1N1 influenza
🔑 Subclinical vs. Latent — High-Yield Distinction
Subclinical: bug IS growing, immune response IS happening, person IS shedding — just no symptoms. Latent: bug is dormant; not detectable; no immune response, no shedding. Both look 'well' clinically — but subclinical people are actively infectious!
🩺 Zoonosis — Two Main Transmission Modes
Hematophagous arthropod vectors (mosquitoes, ticks) OR direct contact/handling of infected animals. Many zoonotic agents (anthrax, smallpox, hemorrhagic fevers) have historically been weaponized.

Q: Can a single disease be classified under multiple categories (e.g., both nosocomial AND contagious)?

Answer

Yes. These categories describe different aspects — where acquired (nosocomial), how easily it spreads (contagious), what immune state required (opportunistic). They are not mutually exclusive.

LO 4

Compare and contrast endemic, epidemic, pandemic, syndemic

Greek roots give you the meaning. Scope is the key differentiator.

  • ✓
    Endemic (endemos = native) → constant baseline in a population/region; e.g., malaria in sub-Saharan Africa
  • ✓
    Epidemic (epidemos = upon the people) → sudden increase above expected baseline; reduced immunity OR novel pathogen
  • ✓
    Pandemic (pandemos = all the people) → epidemic spanning multiple countries; novel pathogen with little immunity
  • ✓
    Syndemic → two or more co-occurring epidemics that interact synergistically (e.g., COVID + flu; HIV + TB)
LO 4

Epidemiological Scale

Endemic → Epidemic → Pandemic → Syndemic

Greek: endemos = "native"

Endemic

Infection constantly maintained at a baseline level in a population or geographic area. Used to guide travel medicine ("Have you visited an endemic area?").

Examples: malaria in sub-Saharan Africa, ETEC in developing regions

Greek: epidemos = "upon the people"

Epidemic

Sudden increase or rapid spread above what is normally expected in that region. Caused by reduced population immunity (e.g., stopping vaccines) OR appearance of a novel pathogen.

Examples: measles outbreaks in unvaccinated communities, H1N1 2009

Greek: pandemos = "all the people"

Pandemic

Epidemic spreading across multiple countries or continents, affecting large numbers. Usually involves a novel pathogen with little or no established immunity.

Examples: COVID-19, 1918 influenza, HIV/AIDS

Greek: syn = "together"

Syndemic

Two or more co-occurring epidemics that interact synergistically, increasing disease burden beyond what either would cause alone. Often linked by social determinants of health.

Examples: COVID + influenza in winter; HIV + TB co-epidemic

💡 Why Epidemics Happen
Two triggers: (1) Reduced immunity to an established pathogen — e.g., stopping vaccination allows diseases to resurge. (2) Novel pathogen introduced to a naive population — e.g., European diseases devastating Native Americans who had zero prior immunity.

Q: COVID-19 caused deaths globally across every continent in 2020. What is the correct epidemiological term, and why?

Answer

Pandemic — it spread across multiple countries and continents, affecting massive numbers, and the causative agent (SARS-CoV-2) was a novel pathogen to which humans had little established immunity.

LO 5

Discuss common modes of microbial transmission

Direct vs. indirect. For indirect: vehicle-borne vs. vector-borne (biological vs. mechanical) vs. airborne. Key: does the organism replicate in the vector?

  • ✓
    Direct: skin/mucosa contact, large respiratory droplets (~1 m range), contaminated soil, inoculation (trauma, bites), transplacental
  • ✓
    Vehicle-borne: food/water, bioproducts (blood, serum, tissue), fomites (inanimate objects) — no replication needed
  • ✓
    Mechanical vector: carried on insect body; no replication → essentially a moving fomite (e.g., flies on food)
  • ✓
    Biological vector: organism REPLICATES in vector → high infection risk on next bite (malaria in mosquito, Lyme in tick)
  • ✓
    Airborne: small particles 1–5 μm; long distance; drying destroys enveloped viruses
  • ✓
    Carrier: asymptomatic host who transmits — e.g., Typhoid Mary (gallbladder reservoir)
LO 5

Microbial Spread

Modes of Transmission

Slide — Direct Transmission Routes

Slide — Indirect Transmission Routes

Direct Transmission

  • Direct contact — touching, kissing, sexual activity
  • Large respiratory droplets — range ~1 m; 'direct' because very close. COVID was primarily this route.
  • Contaminated soil — animal droppings, fungi, environmental bacteria
  • Direct inoculation — trauma, animal bites/scratches, medical procedures
  • Transplacental / Vertical — mother → fetus via placenta; most efficient vertical route

Indirect Transmission

🚗 Vehicle-Borne
Intermediate material carries the organism to a portal of entry. Does NOT need to replicate in the vehicle. Three types: Food/water (cholera, E. coli, Hep A), Bioproducts (contaminated blood/tissue — HIV, HBV, HCV), and Fomites (any inanimate object — cups, bedding, doorknobs, toys).
🦟 Vector-Borne — Biological vs. Mechanical
Biological vector: organism REPLICATES in the vector (malaria in mosquito, EEE). Next bite delivers a high load. True vector-borne disease. Mechanical vector: carried on insect body but does NOT replicate (flies walking on food). Functionally a fomite. HIV cannot replicate in mosquito gut → mosquitoes CANNOT transmit HIV.
💨 Airborne (Aerosol)
Small particles 1–5 μm; remain suspended for extended periods; can travel across a room or building. Bad news for enveloped viruses — aerosols dry quickly and destroy lipid envelopes. This is why droplet transmission is often more efficient for COVID and influenza.
🩺 Carrier State — Typhoid Mary
Mary Mallon had asymptomatic chronic typhoid (Salmonella typhi in gallbladder). She was a cook who transmitted typhoid to wealthy New Yorkers. A cholecystectomy would have cured her carriage but she refused. Carriers = asymptomatic humans or animals who transmit via any route.
RouteReplication Needed in Vehicle/Vector?Examples
Direct contactN/ASTIs, respiratory viruses (droplet)
FomiteNoNorovirus on surfaces, influenza on doorknobs
Food/waterNoCholera, E. coli O157, Hep A, Salmonella
BioproductsNoHIV, HBV, HCV via blood/tissue
Mechanical vectorNoFlies spreading GI pathogens to food
Biological vectorYes (required)Malaria (Anopheles), Lyme (Ixodes), EEE (mosquito)
Airborne (aerosol)NoTB, measles, varicella, aspergillus
TransplacentalN/ATORCH infections (CMV, Toxo, Rubella, HSV)

Q: A person wonders if they can catch HIV from a mosquito bite. How do you explain this?

Answer

No. For biological vector transmission, the organism must replicate in the vector. HIV cannot replicate in the mosquito gut. Additionally, the mosquito only takes ~1/1000 mL of blood, and the quantity of HIV in that volume is negligible. HIV requires direct transmission via sexual contact, blood products, or vertical transmission.

LO 6

Compare and contrast general characteristics of viruses vs. prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes

Viruses are the outliers — not truly alive, obligate intracellular parasites, no ribosomes, no ATP.

  • ✓
    Viruses: 20–300 nm; RNA or DNA (not both); no ribosomes; can't generate ATP; obligate intracellular; host-mediated replication
  • ✓
    Prokaryotes: 0.2–30 μm; DNA + RNA; 70S ribosomes; no membrane-bound nucleus; independent metabolism; 10× faster replication than eukaryotes
  • ✓
    Eukaryotes: membrane-bound nucleus and organelles; 80S ribosomes; independent complex metabolism
  • ✓
    Key: Rickettsia and Chlamydia are also obligate intracellular bacteria BUT can still do limited metabolism — viruses do NOTHING without their host
LO 6

Comparative Microbiology

Virus vs. Prokaryote vs. Eukaryote

Slide — Advantages of Small Size in Prokaryotes

FeatureVirusProkaryote (Bacteria)Eukaryote
Size20–300 nm0.2–30 μm10–100+ μm
Nucleic AcidRNA or DNA (not both)DNA + RNADNA + RNA
NucleusNoneNone (nucleoid)Membrane-bound nucleus
RibosomesNone (uses host)70S80S
Energy (ATP)Cannot generate or storeYes — independent metabolismYes — mitochondria
ReplicationHost-mediated; does not divideBinary fission; independent; ~10× faster than eukaryoteMitosis/meiosis
Intracellular?Obligate intracellularMost extracellular; some obligate (Rickettsia, Chlamydia)No (most)
'Alive'?Debated — not in strict senseYesYes
🔑 Why Prokaryotes Are Highly Competitive
Small size = rapid nutrient/waste exchange + rapid macromolecular synthesis + faster cell division. A prokaryotic cell can grow 10× faster than a single eukaryotic cell. This is why bacteria can outgrow host defenses and establish infection so rapidly.
💡 Viruses — Obligate Intracellular Parasites
Without their host, viruses cannot synthesize proteins (no ribosomes), cannot generate energy (no ATP machinery), and cannot replicate. They parasitize the host cell to get amino acids, nucleotides, and lipids — the host does all the building work, directed by viral mRNA.

Q: Why do viruses only have either RNA or DNA, while bacteria have both?

Answer

Viruses evolved extreme genomic economy — carrying only the minimum genetic information needed to hijack a host cell. Most human pathogenic viruses are single-stranded RNA viruses. They use the host's machinery for everything else. Bacteria, as complete living organisms, need both DNA (genetic storage) and RNA (transcription/translation).

LO 7

Describe general aspects of viral structure, replication, and classification

Know two structural types (naked vs. enveloped), the role of the capsid, and key classification criteria.

  • ✓
    Capsid = protein coat made of capsomeres; protects nucleic acid; binding sites on naked viruses; symmetry = helical or icosahedral
  • ✓
    Envelope = lipid bilayer surrounding nucleocapsid; partly derived from host membrane during budding; LABILE to drying, acid, detergents, UV
  • ✓
    Classification: type of nucleic acid, genome structure, capsid symmetry, envelope presence, size → now supplemented by genomic sequencing
  • ✓
    Most human pathogens = ssRNA viruses (board key fact). DNA virus exceptions: herpes, adeno, pox, HBV, parvovirus B19
  • ✓
    ~20 families of human viruses; each has hundreds of species and multiple serotypes
LO 7

Virology Fundamentals

Viral Structure, Replication & Classification

Slide — Relative Sizes of Viruses

Slide — Components of the Basic Virion

Slide — Virus Genomes: DNA and RNA variations

Viral Structural Components

🛡️

Capsid (All Viruses)

  • Protein shell made of capsomeres
  • Protects nucleic acid from environmental degradation
  • In naked viruses: contains host-binding sites + antigenic determinant
  • May contain fusion proteins to assist host entry
  • Symmetry: helical or icosahedral
🫧

Envelope (Some Viruses)

  • Lipid bilayer surrounding the nucleocapsid
  • Contains glycoproteins (e.g., COVID spike protein)
  • Some lipid derived from host cell membrane (during budding)
  • Antigenic fingerprint = on envelope surface
  • LABILE: disrupted by drying, detergent, acid, UV, solvents
  • Released by budding (not lysis)

Viral Genome Types

Nucleic AcidStrandednessExamples
RNA (most human pathogens)ssRNA+ (acts as own mRNA)Poliovirus, Hep A, Coxsackievirus, Coronaviruses
RNAssRNA− (must synthesize + strand first)Influenza, RSV, Rabies, Measles, Ebola
RNAdsRNARotavirus
DNAdsDNAHerpes (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV), Adenovirus, Poxvirus, HPV
DNAssDNAParvovirus B19
RNA → DNA (retrovirus)ssRNA + reverse transcriptaseHIV, HTLV
🔑 Board Key Fact — Most Human Pathogens = ssRNA
When in doubt on boards, assume single-stranded RNA virus. Learn the DNA exceptions: Herpes viruses (dsDNA), Adenovirus (dsDNA), Poxvirus (dsDNA), Hepatitis B (dsDNA, partially), Parvovirus B19 (ssDNA). Everything else → RNA.
🩺 Enveloped Virus Lability
Enveloped viruses (HIV, influenza, COVID, herpesviruses) are easily killed by soap/detergent, alcohol-based sanitizers, drying, acid pH, and UV light. Naked viruses (norovirus, HAV, poliovirus) are much more resistant — fomite transmission is much more common for naked viruses.

Q: COVID-19 serological tests detect antibodies against the spike protein. Why is this a valid diagnostic target?

Answer

The spike protein is embedded in the lipid envelope (glycoprotein on the envelope surface). For enveloped viruses, the outer envelope is the antigenic fingerprint — the surface structure that stimulates antibody production. Testing for IgG/IgM against spike protein = testing for immune response against the defining antigenic structure of the virus.

LO 8

Compare viral lytic vs. lysogenic replication cycles

Lytic = produce and burst. Lysogenic = integrate and hide/bud. Know the steps and outcomes of each.

  • ✓
    Lytic cycle steps: Attachment → Penetration → Uncoating → Transcription/Replication → Assembly/Maturation → Release (lysis)
  • ✓
    Lytic = naked viruses typically; 500–1000 progeny per cell; host cell destroyed
  • ✓
    Budding/Lysogenic = enveloped viruses typically; cell not immediately destroyed; slower but sustained release
  • ✓
    Attachment: requires receptor-ligand specificity (104–105 binding sites per cell) → explains tissue tropism
  • ✓
    Anti-influenza drugs (neuraminidase inhibitors) block Step 7 — Release
LO 8

Viral Replication

Lytic vs. Lysogenic Replication Cycles

Slide — Multiplication Cycle: Attachment → Penetration → Uncoating → Transcription → Replication → Assembly → Release

Steps of Viral Replication

  1. Attachment (Adsorption) — Random collision; requires specific receptor-ligand binding (104–105 host binding sites per cell). Determines tissue tropism.
  2. Penetration (Entry) — Mechanisms: viropexis (threads through membrane), endocytosis, or fusion. Bacteriophage-style injection is NOT common in human viruses.
  3. Uncoating — Host signals virus to release genome, making it accessible to host transcription/translation machinery.
  4. Early Transcription → mRNA — Viral mRNA produced, coding for early proteins (enzymes, regulatory proteins).
  5. Genome Replication — Viral DNA or RNA replicated. Location varies: cytoplasm, nucleus, or both — depends on virus.
  6. Assembly / Maturation — Nucleic acid packaged into capsid; structural proteins assembled into new virions.
  7. Release — Critically important. Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir) block this step for influenza, trapping virus inside host cells.
💥

Lytic Cycle

  • Typical of naked (non-enveloped) viruses
  • Produces 500–1000 progeny per infected cell
  • Progeny form crystalline arrays inside host
  • Virus weakens cytoskeleton → cell lyses → mass release
  • Host cell is destroyed
  • Rapid, acute damage
  • Examples: poliovirus, adenovirus
🌱

Budding / Lysogenic Release

  • Typical of enveloped viruses
  • Virus buds slowly through host membrane, acquiring lipid envelope
  • Takes fragments of host membrane in the process
  • Host cell not immediately killed — slower damage
  • Allows chronic infection to develop
  • Examples: HIV, herpesviruses, influenza
  • DNA viruses (herpes) can also integrate into chromosome
🔑 Tissue Tropism Explained
If you inject free viral nucleic acid directly into a cell, you might get replication — but progeny CANNOT re-infect because they lack the external binding proteins. Specificity of binding = specificity of infection. GI viruses only infect GI tract; neurotropic viruses only infect neurons — receptor-binding specificity.

Q: Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir) treat influenza. At which step of the replication cycle do they act?

Answer

Step 7 — Release. Neuraminidase is required for influenza virions to bud out of the host cell (cleaves sialic acid linkages). Inhibiting it traps new virions inside the host cell. The immune system then eliminates the infected cells.

LO 9

Describe general processes by which viruses cause disease

Direct cell damage vs. indirect immune-mediated damage. Both can be lethal.

  • ✓
    Direct damage: host synthetic pathways disrupted; cell energy hijacked to build viruses; viral mRNA competes for ribosomes → cell fails
  • ✓
    Indirect — Genomic integration: viral DNA integrates into host chromosome → functional mutations or tumorigenic mutations
  • ✓
    Indirect — Immune/cytokine response: cytokine storm; inflammatory mediators damage host cells (not just pathogen); sepsis = classic example
  • ✓
    Parasite paradox: optimal pathogens don't kill hosts (depletes reservoir). Pandemics from zoonotic spillover are initially very lethal, then moderate as virus adapts to human host
LO 9

Viral Pathogenesis

How Viruses Cause Disease

💔

Direct Cell Damage

  • Host cell synthetic pathways disrupted
  • Energy and macromolecular components hijacked to build viruses
  • Viral mRNA competes with host mRNA for ribosomes
  • In lytic infections: cell is literally destroyed
  • In budding infections: slow but cumulative damage
  • Organ dysfunction when large numbers of cells affected
🔬

Indirect Damage

  • Genomic integration: viral DNA inserts into host chromosome → functional mutations → potentially tumorigenic
  • Cytokine storm: inflammatory mediators directed at pathogen also damage host tissue
  • Sepsis: systemic immune response → host cell collateral damage
  • COVID 'long haul' symptoms partly attributed to immune-mediated damage
🔑 The Parasite Paradox
An ideal parasite does NOT kill its host — if it does, it loses its transmission vehicle. Pandemics from zoonotic spillover (COVID from bats) are initially very lethal because the virus isn't adapted to humans. Over time, variants that killed everyone ran out of hosts. Evolution favors transmissibility over lethality.

Q: A patient in septic shock from influenza has worsening organ failure despite antiviral therapy. What indirect pathogenic mechanism is contributing?

Answer

Cytokine storm / immune-mediated damage. The patient's own immune response is releasing massive quantities of inflammatory cytokines that, while directed at the virus, cause collateral damage to host tissues including the endothelium and kidneys. This is why immunomodulatory therapy (e.g., corticosteroids in severe COVID) is sometimes needed alongside antivirals.

LO 10

Distinguish acute, latent, and chronic forms of viral infection

Three distinct outcomes. Latent is most misunderstood — no viral replication detectable, but genome persists silently.

  • ✓
    Acute: multiple rounds of replication + host cell death → thousands of progeny → immune clearance or host death
  • ✓
    Latent: no (or minimal) viral replication; genome present episomally or integrated; no symptoms; can reactivate (stress, immunosuppression, UV light)
  • ✓
    Chronic: sustained low-level viral replication; progeny released without immediate cell death; damage accumulates over years (HBV, HCV → cirrhosis)
  • ✓
    Herpes latency location: dorsal root ganglia; reactivation → shingles in dermatomal distribution
LO 10

Viral Infection Outcomes

Acute, Latent & Chronic Viral Infections

Slide — Outcomes of Viral Infection: Acute, Latent, Chronic

TypeReplication LevelCell Death?SymptomsViral Examples
Acute LyticHigh — multiple roundsYes — massiveAcute illness; resolves with immune clearance or host deathInfluenza, poliovirus, rhinovirus
LatentNone (or undetectable)NoNone during latency; symptoms only on reactivationHSV-1/2, VZV (chickenpox/shingles), CMV, EBV
ChronicLow-level, sustainedSlow/delayedMinimal initially; progressive damage over yearsHBV, HCV, HIV
💡 Latent Infection — Two Mechanisms
Two mechanisms of herpesvirus latency: (1) Episomal — viral genome sits as circular DNA in the cytoplasm, replicated during cell division. (2) Chromosomal integration — viral DNA integrates into host chromosome, replicated with every cell division. During latency, infectious virus is NOT produced and person is NOT contagious. Reactivation re-initiates the lytic cycle.
🩺 Herpes Latency — Dorsal Root Ganglia
VZV causes chickenpox on primary infection, then establishes latency in the dorsal root ganglia. Decades later, reactivation causes shingles in the dermatomal distribution of the affected ganglion. Shingrix (recombinant vaccine) recommended for adults ≥50.
🩺 Chronic Hepatitis — Years to Cirrhosis
Chronic HBV and HCV produce low-level continuous viremia over years to decades. Slowly, infected hepatocytes are damaged, fibrous tissue replaces them, and cirrhosis develops. The patient may have no symptoms for 20+ years before presenting with end-stage liver disease.

Q: A patient with a history of childhood chickenpox develops a painful vesicular rash along one side of the chest. What is the mechanism?

Answer

Reactivation of latent VZV causing shingles. After primary chickenpox, VZV established latency in the dorsal root ganglion. Reactivation (triggered by immunosenescence, stress, or immunosuppression) allows the virus to travel down sensory nerve fibers to the skin, causing the characteristic dermatomal vesicular rash and post-herpetic neuralgia.

LO 11

Identify and describe rash-causing viral exanthems by clinical presentation and etiological agent

High-yield for boards. Know the rash type, virus, key presentation, and distinguishing features. Skin tone matters for exam images.

  • ✓
    Measles (Rubeola) → Paramyxovirus (ssRNA); maculopapular; cough + coryza + conjunctivitis (3 C's); Koplik spots pathognomonic
  • ✓
    Fifth Disease (Erythema infectiosum) → Parvovirus B19 (ssDNA); 'slapped cheek' face; lacy trunk rash; risk in pregnancy → hydrops fetalis
  • ✓
    Roseola (6th disease / Exanthem subitum) → HHV-6 (dsDNA herpesvirus); high fever then maculopapular rash on trunk; NOT vesicular despite being herpes ⭐
  • ✓
    Varicella (Chickenpox) → VZV = Herpes 3 (dsDNA); vesicular; multiple stages at once; latency in dorsal root ganglia → shingles on reactivation
  • ✓
    Hand-Foot-Mouth → Coxsackievirus A16 (ssRNA Enterovirus); vesicles on palms/soles/oral mucosa; August–September daycare outbreaks
  • ✓
    Herpes Simplex → HSV-1/2 (dsDNA); vesicular; HSV-1 ≠ only oral; HSV-2 ≠ only genital — either type can appear anywhere
LO 11

Pediatric & Adult Viral Rashes

Viral Exanthems

An exanthem is an eruptive rash accompanying viral infection. Extremely common in unvaccinated children; increasingly seen again with declining vaccination rates.

Slide — Rash Types shown on varying skin tones

Rash Type Definitions

TypeDescription
MaculeFlat, circumscribed area lighter or darker than surrounding skin; no elevation
PapuleSmall raised bump, typically <1 cm
PustulePapule containing pus
MaculopapularMixed: flat macules + raised papules together; most common viral rash type; may start as macular and evolve
VesicularBlisters filled with clear fluid (not pus)

1. Measles (Rubeola)

Slide — Measles: Maculopapular rash + Koplik spots

🔑 Measles (Rubeola)
  • Virus: Paramyxovirus (ssRNA, ~200–250 nm)
  • Presentation: High fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis (3 C's)
  • Rash: Starts macular → maculopapular; face/trunk → extremities
  • PATHOGNOMONIC: Koplik spots — white papules on red base on buccal mucosa; if you see them, it's measles
  • Easier to see on light skin; look carefully on darker skin

2. Fifth Disease (Erythema Infectiosum)

Slide — Erythema infectiosum: 'Slapped Cheek' presentation

💡 Fifth Disease (Parvovirus B19)
  • Virus: Parvovirus B19 (ssDNA — one of the few DNA viruses here!)
  • Presentation: Runny nose, conjunctivitis, low-grade fever
  • Rash: Classic 'slapped cheek' bright erythema on face → lacy/reticular rash on trunk/extremities
  • Common in children; no vaccine available
  • ⚠️ Dangerous in pregnancy: hydrops fetalis (fetal anemia → heart failure)
  • Harder to see on darker skin

3. Roseola (Exanthem Subitum / 6th Disease) — HIGH YIELD ⭐

Slide — Roseola: Maculopapular trunk rash after high fever

⭐ Roseola — Board Favorite!
  • Virus: Human Herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6) — dsDNA herpesvirus
  • Classic pattern: High fever (3–5 days) → fever breaks → maculopapular rash on trunk → extremities
  • Rash may be missed on darker skin
  • Board trap: HHV-6 = herpesvirus but causes maculopapular rash, NOT vesicular!
  • If board says 'Roseola' → answer is HHV-6

4. Varicella / Shingles (VZV = Herpes 3)

Slide — Varicella: Vesicular rash (chickenpox)

Slide — Shingles: Dermatomal distribution

🩺 VZV — Chickenpox & Shingles
  • Virus: Varicella-Zoster Virus = Herpes type 3 (dsDNA)
  • Primary (Chickenpox): Itchy vesicular rash; lesions in multiple stages at once (fluid-filled and crusted simultaneously); spreads centripetally from trunk
  • Latency: VZV establishes latency in dorsal root ganglia
  • Reactivation (Shingles): Dermatomal vesicular rash + severe pain; post-herpetic neuralgia; obvious regardless of skin tone due to pain + distribution
  • Vaccinate: varicella vaccine for children; Shingrix for adults ≥50

5. Hand, Foot & Mouth Disease

Slide — Hand, Foot & Mouth: Vesicular rash on hands and feet

💡 Hand, Foot & Mouth (Coxsackievirus)
  • Virus: Coxsackievirus A16 (ssRNA, Enterovirus)
  • Presentation: Vesicular rash on palms, soles, oral mucosa (and sometimes buttocks)
  • Sore throat + oral ulcers common
  • Epidemiology: Highly contagious; August–September outbreaks in daycare settings
  • Self-limited; supportive care only; no specific antiviral

6. Herpes Simplex (HSV-1 & HSV-2)

Slide — Herpes Simplex: Classic vesicular rash

🔬 Herpes Simplex (HSV-1/2)
  • Virus: HSV-1 & HSV-2 — dsDNA (episomal and chromosomally integrated)
  • Rash: Classic clustered vesicular lesions
  • HSV-1 = traditionally oral (cold sores); HSV-2 = traditionally genital
  • However: either type can appear at either site — location ≠ type!
  • Latency in sensory ganglia; reactivates with stress, fever, UV, immunosuppression
  • Treated with acyclovir, valacyclovir

Q: A 2-year-old has a temperature of 40°C for 4 days. The fever breaks on day 5 and a maculopapular rash appears on the trunk. What is the diagnosis and causative agent?

Answer

Roseola (Exanthem Subitum / 6th disease), caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), a dsDNA herpesvirus. Classic: high fever 3–5 days → fever breaks abruptly → maculopapular rash appears on trunk. Students often miss this because it's a herpesvirus but causes a maculopapular (not vesicular) rash.

Q: A pregnant healthcare worker is exposed to a child with fifth disease. Why is this concerning?

Answer

Fifth disease is caused by Parvovirus B19 (ssDNA). In pregnant women, maternal Parvovirus B19 can cross the placenta and infect fetal red blood cell precursors (erythroblasts), causing severe fetal anemia → high-output cardiac failure → hydrops fetalis (fetal edema, ascites, pleural effusions). Life-threatening for the fetus, especially in the 1st and 2nd trimesters.
